Phase 07 · 7–10 hours + kiln cycles

Fire & diagnose.

The kiln is not a verdict delivered by magic. Learn to reconstruct what happened from event, location, material records, witness cones, and physical evidence.

Start before the kilnOpen the defect atlas

Aim

From “it cracked” to a testable explanation.

Prerequisite

Documented making and surface tests; access to an authorized kiln operator or supervised studio.

By the end

You can distinguish drying and firing evidence, read cones as heatwork, build competing hypotheses, and make conservative use decisions.

Deliverables

A drying comparison, firing record, defect atlas, evidence diagnosis, and functional-use decision.

07.1

Many apparent kiln failures begin earlier.

If a pot breaks in the kiln, what evidence shows whether the cause was moisture, construction, handling, or firing?

Diagnostic frame

Event × location × evidence

When was the change first observed? Where did it occur? What physical trace and process record support the claim? A cause is stronger when it predicts the fracture path or defect pattern.

The moisture distinction

Air itself is not the standard explanation for “exploding pots.” Residual water turning to steam, thick or uneven sections, restricted escape paths, and aggressive early heating are central concerns. Follow your studio’s drying and firing protocols.

Lab · Drying comparison45 min + drying

Before making hollow forms, learn your studio’s limits for thickness, mass, internal drying access, and vents. A vent supports drying and inspection; it does not make damp ware safe. Never leave unapproved metal, foil, plastic, wood, plaster, or other objects inside ordinary kiln work. Make three matched hollow test forms with safe vent paths. Dry one evenly covered, one with the rim exposed, and one on a nonabsorbent support. Weigh or measure them at consistent intervals if possible.

  1. Map color and firmness differences.
  2. Record where cracks initiate and their direction.
  3. Relate the evidence to geometry and moisture gradient. Do not fire intentionally damp ware.
Studio safety: kiln loading, programs, ventilation, maintenance, and hot unloading are for trained, authorized people following equipment and studio rules. Keep combustible materials clear and never bypass interlocks.
07.2

Cones measure heatwork, not a fixed temperature.

Heatwork reflects the combined effect of temperature and time on ceramic materials. A witness cone bends in response to that work near the ware. A controller reading and a cone tell related but different stories.

Cone number matters

Cone 06 and cone 6 are far apart. The leading zero marks a lower range; never drop it in notes or labels.

Atmosphere matters

Oxidation, reduction, airflow, and vapor affect color and chemistry. Record the actual studio process rather than assuming.

Location matters

Shelves and zones can receive different heatwork. Record placement so repeated variation becomes diagnosable.

Practice · Read a firing record60 min

Using a studio firing you are permitted to observe, record kiln ID, date, program or schedule, target cone, witness-cone result by zone, atmosphere, load notes, and cooling notes. Pair every test tile with its exact location.

Explain one discrepancy between controller data and cones without treating either as infallible.

07.3

Diagnose patterns, not names.

EvidenceCompeting explanationsUseful next test
Crack follows joinWeak integration; moisture mismatch; drying stressMatched seam coupons with controlled drying
Fine glaze networkFit mismatch; delayed stress; intentional crackle systemKnown tile series; studio-approved fit/use evaluation
Glaze crawls into islandsDust/grease; poor adhesion; thick application; shrinkageCleanliness and application-thickness comparison
Pinholes or cratersGas release; glaze maturity; application; firing/coolingRepeat tiles with controlled layer and firing position
Body warpsMaking stress; uneven support; heatwork; pyroplastic movementProcess-matched tiles by orientation and kiln zone
Sharp glaze flakes / shiveringGlaze–body fit; edge geometry; process historyReject from use; stop this combination and seek technical review
Steam damage or blowoutResidual moisture; thick/closed section; aggressive early heatDo not refire; review drying evidence and firing protocol
Straight late fracture / duntingThermal stress or cooling; prior flawCompare fracture, timing, form geometry, and firing record
Bloating or softened bodyGas during vitrification; excess heatwork; body incompatibilityCheck cones, body range, and kiln zone
Dry/porous or slumped/runnyUnderfire or overfire; application; wrong rangeVerify materials and cones before a controlled repeat
Glaze runExcess thickness, layering, heatwork, or formulationProtect shelves and test at smaller scale; do not normalize the defect
Make · Defect atlas90 min

For four real examples, include photographs from two angles, event first observed, location, materials, firing record, two plausible causes, evidence for/against each, and the smallest safe test that separates them.

Fracture clues are not proof.Glaze inside a crack can suggest it predated glaze melt; a clean sharp fracture can suggest later breakage, but neither is infallible. “Refire hotter” is not a generic repair: refiring can worsen fit, running, bloating, deformation, color, and dimensions. Stay within material limits and use a controlled test.
Repair conservatively.Cosmetic repair does not automatically restore structural or functional integrity. Remake compromised load-bearing or food-contact ware unless a qualified studio protocol supports another decision.
07.4

Project: evidence-based use decision.

Integrated diagnosis

Use, retest, repurpose, or reject?

Select one finished piece with a concern. Make a defensible decision for its intended use without claiming certainty your evidence cannot support.

  1. Document clay, surface materials, construction, drying, firing, kiln location, and intended use.
  2. Describe the concern precisely by pattern, size, location, timing, and change over time.
  3. Generate at least two hypotheses and identify disconfirming evidence for each.
  4. Consult studio guidance or qualified technical support where functional safety is implicated.
  5. Choose: use as intended, limited nonfood use, display/test only, remake, or discard according to studio policy. State why.

Inspiration · look comparatively

Fire transforms material—and kiln architecture shapes the conditions.

Compare glaze response with two historic approaches to containing heat. Both kiln photographs are context, not operating guidance; follow authorized studio procedures and equipment-specific instruction.

Knowledge check · 3 questions

Pause. Predict. Diagnose.

Choose one answer for each situation. Open a hint when needed; explanations appear after you check all three.
